utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. A very good afternoon to everybody. May we please hear the case number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian, Ann Sutherland, and Ruth Karper for the Office of the Prosecutor. And Happy New Year to the Defence and all those who celebrate according to the Orthodox calendar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence. And I thank the Prosecution for their wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I apologise for having been not aware of the fact and, no doubt on behalf of the entire Chamber, we as well wish a very good and prosperous New Year for those who celebrate according to the Orthodox calendar. Before we start today, the hearings of today, it was on purpose that yesterday I decided not to declare once again closed, the Prosecution's case, and did not excuse Witness Sivac, but I take it from the fact that I got no contacts from the parties, that there is anything in addition that would give a reason for a continuous hearing of Mr. Sivac. So therefore, now Mr. Sivac is excused formally, and at the same time, we are now once again within the Defence case. I deplore that I have to come back to an issue that we discussed yesterday. This is the presentation of documents in due time and in due form, including translation. Yesterday, after a long discussion, we heard from the Defence their apologies in part about certain issues just discussed recently, but then we experienced that we were taken once again by surprise by another document, by a document which was undoubtedly in the hands of the Defence a period of time ago. And the Defence even presented a number of questions to be put to this witness in advance, without announcing that there would be such a new exhibit. And this exhibit was not translated; it was not understandable; it was not well founded. It was just a kind of guessing game. And it was also, in a way, aggressive against a witness. I think it should be quite clear that it is also for us to protect the interests of witnesses. No doubt that in case the Defence feels it necessary to demonstrate or to prove that a witness is not capable to, or was at that time not capable, for example, to see a certain person due to the fact that he needed glasses and he had not the necessary glasses, that this can form part of the cross-examination. But what cannot be allowed is really to intimidate a witness without any foundation. And as we heard yesterday, there was a document provided from a health centre - I don't want to go into any detail whether it's the same hospital presided over earlier by the accused in this case - and used these documents, in fact, even against a witness, a witness we have to protect, and without any substantiation what the content of this document means. This may amount to an unethical behaviour from the side of the Defence. The Trial Chamber decided not to go into any investigations on the source of this document and the content of this document. The document has only got a concrete number. It was marked, but it will never be used as evidence in this case. There is no probative value for this case. Second, how can we avoid that this happens in future again? Maybe in future the Prosecution would require a postponement of the hearing of a witness until they have had the possibility to go into the details of the new and surprising evidence. And it would give reason enough for the Prosecution to ask for this postponement. The same could be true for the Chamber; the Chamber could need some time for preparation. But we want to emphasise, after deliberations, that in case such a delay will occur, it will be on the account of the Defence. There will be no day longer for the Defence case when such a delay is more or less deliberately caused by the Defence. This, of course, does not mean that the case may happen that a witness comes with a new exhibit with new evidence and the Defence wants immediately to tender this evidence. This may be, and this happened in the past and this can happen in the future. But then, please, good cause may be shown and the reason may be shown. This brings me to the third point: We have the proffer before us. I don't think that we need to revisit the question of proffers. I believe it was understood by the parties. But with a view to today's witness, may I ask the Defence, what is your realistic expectation on the time you need, based on your proffer, for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We estimated the direct examination of this witness, as you know, Your Honours, being four and four and a half hours, but yesterday we were asked to shorten this period, and we'll do our best. So we think that it may be that we'll finish this witness in three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admittedly, it's still surprisingly long, based on that what we can read from the proffer. So no doubt we proceed as we did in the Prosecution's case. But please, be not surprised that the Chamber takes the liberty to ask you at a certain point of time to concentrate on the relevant portions, relevant for this case, and I want also to ask the Prosecution to do that what's apt for the other party, to intervene if they feel there's no relevance. Any other comments on the points raised by the Chamber, or other issues before we start hearing the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I just want to notify the Chamber that the interview of Mrs. Plavsic is available in Court now and can be distributed at the break and has been provided to the Defence earlier today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, the entire agreement is included?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'll review that before the break to answer Your Honour's question. I believe the factual basis was a public document, and that's not included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'll review what we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Because you will understand that it's absolutely necessary that we know what is and what was the basis of this agreement and whether it has any kind of impact on our case, or may it tend to have an impact, to be more on the safe side. Thank you. I can't see anybody asking for the floor. May I then ask, any changes as regards the protective measures related to the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. There is no changes relating to the protective measures. Only maybe we would ask kindly to discuss the scheduling order, because as we glanced through the document, we wouldn't have any chance to meet with the client if we continue to be in a courtroom the whole day every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is in an absolutely different issue, and it should be taken care that the witness doesn't appear in the courtroom when we are discussing this issue. As regards this week, it was necessary because of the order of the President to have an extraordinary plenary, first scheduled for tomorrow, then next week, but in this week it will be only -- the sitting will be in the morning in the ordinary period of time. But related to the other weeks, it's in fact that we will have the hearings until 4.30, just in order to allow, in this case, the Defence to have more time for their witnesses as it has shown in the past that -- I remember very well your first initial statement somewhere in April that your witnesses would take us 15 minutes. I was already at that time hesitant, and I'm quite sure it was just an overstatement. But nevertheless, it's necessary to make use of all of the time available for us, and there will be unforeseeable obstacles, impediments in the future no doubt, and therefore we have to make use of the courtroom whenever possible. If there should be an obstacle where, for example, there is no possibility to meet with your client in this week, then please let me know that I can find a possibility with the responsible persons in this premises that, in fact, what is necessary, you can do your job in the appropriate way, and this means that you have enough time in the evening to come together with your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this will be guaranteed. The next witness is standing outside the door, I heard. So please, may I ask the usher now to escort the witness into the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Thank you for coming. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And could you please be so kind and give us your solemn declaration. You find the text there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You are called as a witness for the Defence. Mr. Lukic, the witness is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mrs. Dakic.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record, please, would you state your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Borislava Dakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When were you born, Mrs. Dakic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of November, 1955.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: In Jelicka, in the territory of Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where do you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: In Omarska, in the territory of Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is your occupation, and where do you work?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: I have a degree in law, and I work at the Prijedor health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe for us the situation in Prijedor prior to the 30th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Well, the situation was normal -- actually, I don't think I understand your question. What exactly do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any changes in terms of interethnic relations in light of the overall situation in the former Yugoslavia with respect to the war that was going on in Croatia and Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. My friends, my colleagues, people I worked with, as early as in May 1991 - I'm referring to the events that took place in Slovenia at the time - started expressing some different opinions. And in our conversations, we no longer agreed as to what should be done. I am referring to the arguments that there should be no secession from Yugoslavia, and that the -- what was going on in Croatia in 1991 was not right. My colleagues of Muslim ethnicity, in September 1991, openly expressed hostility towards the Yugoslav People's Army, that is, to our friends and acquaintances who responded to the mobilisation. Our views were no longer the same. I was still personally in favour of the former Yugoslavia, the country where I lived, the country which I loved, and I loved my friends regardless of their ethnicity. However, I could observe that something strange was going on, in particular, in early March and later in April 1992, when my colleagues, my lady friends who worked with me, started leaving with some very banal explanations, such as that they were going to visit their husbands in Zagreb. They would take their children with them, and they would never come back to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there mass departures of the population of Prijedor, and which part of the population left and how?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: During the month of April 1992, departures of the Muslim population were getting massive, on large scale. And every morning, you could see in the centre of Prijedor town, which is located between the football stadium, the social work centre and the department store, and outside the Balkan Hotel and in front of the bus station, you could see several buses lined up and people boarding those buses. In view of the fact that Prijedor is not a very big town, every one of us knew at least a couple of those people who were leaving. I was able to observe this on several occasions. And every morning before I came to work during the month of April, one of my colleagues -- one or two of my colleagues would not show up to work. Specifically, I am referring to Sabiha Music, who was my boss. As we were having coffee that morning, on the 15th of April, she told us that her children will no longer go to school, would stop going to school, that she would take some time off and go to Zagreb in order to pay a visit to her husband who was working in Zagreb at the time. She left on that day, and I never saw her -- I've never seen her again from that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You worked in Prijedor and you lived in Omarska. How did you commute between Omarska and Prijedor at the time? That is, prior to the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: I always went to work by car. However, at the beginning of April, this type of commuting was no longer very safe, so I would leave my car at home and travel by bus -- and travel by train. Between Prijedor and Omarska, there is an 11-kilometre long territory inhabited by Muslim population. Up until April 1992, there had never been any problems there and I travelled normally, safely, as I did through any other area. After all, I worked there. However, at that time, I started observing between Petrov Gaj and Prijedor, in the town of Trnopolje, next to the railway station, in early morning hours, I started observing men wearing green caps, which we called "Green Berets" because after all, those were berets. For a while, they did not carry any weapons. However, later on, I noticed that they had some weapons. I'm not familiar with weapons, and I don't think I could tell you what kind of rifles those were, whether they were automatic rifles or some other types of rifles; I don't know, but I'm sure that those were rifles. And in those days, it was much more comfortable and safer for me to travel by train where there were many more people. Although we were never stopped by anyone, nor did anyone say anything to us in particular; Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. however, on the Banja Luka/Prijedor main road, there were already skirmishes and roadblocks, and also, because I'm a woman, I didn't dare travel around by car. I simply didn't feel safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This feeling of insecurity was also reflected in the fact that you, as you have told me, had packed a certain number of your personal belongings in case of emergency.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: When my boss, whom I mentioned earlier on, went on leave, when she packed her things and left for Zagreb with her children, that moment, although she had never said in particular to me, although we had never discussed the subject, I realised that something was going on, something which didn't augur well. And knowing what could happen, I just collected all of our important personal documents, documents belonging to my husband, my children, and myself, including property deeds, our diplomas, certificates on the completion of our education, and a number of other personal effects which I packed in one bag and which remained packed like that for a couple of years. This would have been the only thing that I would have taken with me if I had had to leave. Those were the things that I considered to be necessary and indispensable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you unpack this bag?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Several months after the signing of the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now focus on the period between the 30th of April and the 30th of September, 1992. If you can talk about the events in view of this chronology. What was going on in May, if you know, after the 30th of April, 1992; that is, after the takeover? We know that on that day, the SDS took over in Prijedor. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Nothing was significantly different between the 28th, 29th of April, or the 1st, 2nd, or the 3rd of May. Everything remained the same on my way to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was anyone sacked from work?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did the problems in the Prijedor Municipality start? You don't have to give us the exact dates, but just tell us, when do you think these problems started?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: I think they started on a Friday, which I believe was the 22nd of May, when an open attack took place, perpetrated by members of the -- I don't know whether those were Muslim forces or simply members of the Muslim population, who attacked a soldier in the village of Hambarine. And at the same time, there were certain minor clashes in Prijedor, such as the attack on the military warehouse which my cousin told me about who, the night before, was standing guard next to this warehouse which is located not far from the local barracks. But there were other things that took place even earlier, perhaps even as early as in April 1992. However, it was on that particular Friday that it became clear to me that ugly things were going to happen, that people no longer had any qualms about taking up arms and that they paid no attention as to whether other people were guilty of anything or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then after that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Well, after that Saturday, Sunday, the roadblocks were set up in the area of I think Kevljani or Kamicani. And again, I think one of the soldiers - I think his name was Kolundija - was killed. Whether there were any other people with him or what was the general outcome, I'm not sure. However, after the attack on the soldiers at Hambarine, the military intervened, and the fighting started. As far as I'm concerned, fighting means opening fire from all sides, irrespective of where the sides are. But I could tell that there were two sides opposed in this conflict, and I could hear shooting from my house. Whether one could call it an armed conflict or something else, I don't know. But as far as I'm concerned, it was a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you continue to go to work at that time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Those days after the 22nd, no, I no longer went to work. There was a weekend, Saturday, Sunday; and then on Monday, there was no possibility for me to go to work because of this armed conflict. And I simply didn't dare travel across the territory which was -- where there was this conflict going on. However, because I knew that my boss would have to reach a decision on the termination of my employment if I don't show up within five days, on the fourth day, with the assistance of a friend of mine who likewise didn't dare to travel across this area, nor did he dare to go along the Banja Luka/Prijedor Road or Omarska/Prijedor Road, but instead took the route via Busnovi, Rakelici, and Maricka, and reached the Muslim area, the area of Cela but which where at the time there were no extremists or other sentiments expressed, through this area, one could get through the checkpoints relatively safely. And this is how I managed to come to work on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is Cela a mixed village?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: I think that one part of Cela used to be purely Muslim, but the neighbouring villages, called Muslimanska Gomjenica, and then the next one, Srpska Gomjenica, Kamicani, Rakici, to what extent this area was mixed in the neighbouring villages, I don't know because I don't know very well this particular area of Prijedor Municipality. However, I am sure that there were no clear-cut boundaries, that their properties and lots were probably interspersed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, you're telling us that at the time, there were no conflicts, no problems in that area.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Until what time did you work in Prijedor, and how did you travel to work?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: I worked for the remainder of the month of May, and also in June. I travelled as best as I could. The public transport no longer functioned, so I would rely on my acquaintances and neighbours who travelled by car, by truck, and who were willing to give me a lift to Prijedor if they could. If not, we would wait for someone else. The trains and buses no longer ran, so it was quite difficult, and it involved crossing the territory where fighting was still going on. But the incidents usually took place by night. However, the next morning, we had to go to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At one point in time, did you stop going to work to Prijedor because you were assigned to work in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did this happen, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: I believe it happened in September or maybe in late August. I know that I went to Prijedor throughout the summer, but then my chief and the supervisor of my department sent me to Omarska, because the winter was approaching and they needed my type of work in this particular work unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, from September -- from April until September 1992, what was the situation like as far as health is concerned? What was the situation with medicines and other supplies?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: The situation was terrible. We were cut off. At that time, there was no corridor towards Yugoslavia. Croatia, of course, we couldn't go there. And you know what such a situation -- what it means for the work of a medical -- medical centre, because there were no factories that were producing medical supplies; medical equipment and medicines alike. And after all, there was war going on, a lot of people were getting sick and wounded. And I know that at that time, as far as medicines are concerned, most of them were often brought by Serbs who were temporarily employed abroad. But before the corridor with Yugoslavia was opened, unfortunately, we were not able to obtain oxygen, let alone other things. A friend of mine whom -- Ljiljana Stjepic, who gave birth in Banja Luka at that time, had a terrible tragedy. She had her baby at that time, but there was no electricity or oxygen and her baby could not be placed in an incubator, and as a result, the baby's vital functions were impaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Later on, when the situation got somewhat better, did you travel to -- through Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see people freely leaving and entering the compound of the elementary school there?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. This could be seen by anyone passing by.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, could counsel refrain from asking leading questions during the period April to September 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Dismissed because in the past we accepted, in this framework, leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I really don't know how to ask differently. I asked, "Did you..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The objection is dismissed, and therefore you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks. Still, I tried to explain. Thanks. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So how did you see these people? Were they there in groups? What was it that you were able to observe in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "in groups"?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, for example, see a larger group of people located next to the elementary school building?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you also see people moving around outside the compound of the elementary school and the community centre?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, within this compound, the compound of the elementary school in Trnopolje, there were many people. However, I saw members of their families who had remained behind at home and who would go to Trnopolje and back. Trnopolje is situated some 6 or 7 kilometres away from Prijedor. You don't need any particular transport to go there. I ran into a colleague of mine, for instance, Mile Hopovac, on one occasion. She travelled on the same train as I did and she told me that she had members of her family who were there, and she told me that she was taking some things to them, and that after that, she would go back home. And when I asked her what they were doing there, she said: "We would like to leave." Obviously this was a very unsafe area for her and for myself as well. But she said: "If we go to Trnopolje and if we are registered there, then it will be easier for us to leave the territory of Republika Srpska." That is, Bosnia and Herzegovina. I didn't ask anything else of her. She got off the train at the station, and I continued on my way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The people who were doing their work obligation or who were -- who were under work obligation or who were mobilised by the army, were they able to leave freely the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it necessary for them to obtain some authorisations or passes to leave the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Well, of course all men who had their military assignment were required to obtain such a permission from the relevant ministry, and they also had to explain why it was necessary for them to leave the territory of Republika Srpska for a while and for how long. Without such a piece of paper, one could not leave. This applied to myself as well, because I was under the so-called work obligation, and I could not cross the border of the country without an authorisation to leave the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who issued such authorisations at the time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: They were issued by the Ministry of Defence. And I think that for a while, they were issued by the Ministry of the Interior; that is, the public security centre in Prijedor was actually closer to where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Still on the issue of dismissals from work, were all people who failed to show up at work for about five days dismissed?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. These employees, however, had the right to object to the decision, the decision on the termination of their employment. Their objections could be reviewed because I know that there are people who received such decisions on the termination of employment at one point in time, but they are still working. So I'm sure that they took it up on a higher level which then examined their particular case and accepted their objections and probably accepted the reasons they provided as to why they failed to show up at work for five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the number of employees officially decreased?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you ever temporarily laid off prior or after April 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was on the so-called waiting list on one occasion before April 1992, but also for a while in 1993 for the following reason: During 1989, 1990, and 1991, there were too many employees and not enough work. And the administration board of the medical centre decided at one point in time that it would be more profitable for a certain number of employees to stop coming to work for a limited period of time, two or three months, for instance. They would be given some salary, not as much as they received normally, but they received some payment. And this was the case with me as well for a while. I was on the so-called waiting list Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in 1989 at one point in time, but also in 1993 the same thing happened. After the outbreak of the conflict in 1992, there was a new staffing table that was made at the health centre, which was adapted to the new war circumstances. And it was the assessment of my boss that at the time, in 1993, there was not enough work for me. So again I was temporarily out of work from May or June 1993 until the 10th of December, 1993. But I was not the only one; there were other similar cases, and it was considered to be a normal phenomenon at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the end of May 1992, were people automatically laid off or would they wait for these decisions, appropriate decisions, to be issued?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: When the war broke out, we were all scared. I have already told you that I didn't dare go to work on day one, and I was not the only one who was scared. We were all scared, and I believe that my Muslim colleagues were even more scared than I was. And none of them came on that first day, but the majority of them failed to come for several more days. I felt more safe, maybe, and I took that bypass road. Maybe I did that because I knew what to expect if I didn't show up for work. But many people failed to show up for work for a number of days. Heads of departments of the health centre at the time did not immediately issue termination papers. They waited -- as far as I could tell, they waited for a few days. I would even come across some of our employees in my offices who would show up from time to time but then they failed to turn up for work either on that day or on the following day. Whether they just came to make some inquiries, whether they came to talk to their heads or what, I don't know. It was not in the nature of my work to attend such conversations, if there were any. However, as time went by, the decision was made that a law, which was valid in the territory of all of Bosnia and Herzegovina, should be applied. And this is the decision that was also applied and the law that was applied even before the war: If you failed to turn up for work for five days, then your employment would be terminated automatically. This is what was happening in January, April, May, and it also happened in the year 1990, 1991. We applied the same law; we applied the provisions of that same law. I don't know why, but I assumed that my acquaintances, my friends and colleagues, and all the other employees of the health centre most probably were too scared to come to work. They feared for their safety. However, even if that was true, their employment was still terminated. It had to be terminated regardless of the reasons for which they didn't show up for work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are there still records of the people who show up for work and why is that necessary?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I believe that it is normal all over the world. Once you start working, somebody has to make sure that you do show up for work. How else could you be paid?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did it all influence anything else but the salary? Did it maybe influence the payment into the pension fund or the health-care fund?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Of course. If you don't show up for work, you don't receive your salary, you don't receive your health-care contribution, your child support contribution, and all the other contributions that are provided for by the law of that specific country. In other words, it is impossible to organise work if your employees do not show up for work. How can you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you personally, as a legal professional, participate in the procedure to terminate the employment of the employees of the health centre?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: In 1992, no, I wasn't involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After September 1992, when Dr. Stakic came to the Prijedor health centre, what position did he come to? So far, there have been some misunderstandings in this trial as regards the dates when Dr. Stakic started working at the health centre and stopped working there.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic came as a doctor to the health centre in Prijedor. That was probably in 1989, but I'm not sure. You can check that in the records of the employee. He worked in the Omarska surgery until the moment he was appointed the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. I believe that that was in 1990. After the election, that was -- it may have even been in the early 1990. At the time, I really did not pay attention to that. I know that there were elections and that the municipal officials were elected, but when they started working there, I don't know. But as from that time on, he was in that position, and he returned to the health centre of Prijedor in May, on the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: 1993, and he was appointed the deputy chief executive officer of the health centre. On that same date, Dr. Milan Kovacevic was appointed the chief executive officer of the health centre, the director of the health centre. And Dr. Stakic remained in the position of the deputy CEO until the end of 1994 when, pursuant to the decision of the government of Republika Srpska, there was a reorganisation of the health centre, and the health centre was divided into the secondary health care and into the primary health care. Dr. Kovacevic was appointed director of the general hospital, and as of the 1st of January, 1995, the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor appointed Dr. Milomir Stakic as the director of the health centre, as the chief executive officer of the health centre. He remained in that position until 1997 or 1998 when he was succeeded by a new director who was then appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1993, when he came to the health centre again, did Dr. Stakic -- had he previously been mobilised into the army, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that he had been, because all of our doctors were mobilised, and they all had their military assignment I couldn't tell you anything of. They would be assigned to a duty for 15 days or 7 days or even up to a month. If you came to work, you could see that somebody was missing, and then he would reappear. I really couldn't know when he was on duty for the military. But all of our doctors were -- had military assignment. You obviously know that, during any war conflict, there should be a person who can administer first aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that he went to the hospitals which were on the front lines?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As a recruitment official, do you know who was in charge of recruitments in the health centre?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Sadeta Grandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did she discharge the same duty during the time while Dr. Stakic was your employee?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that she is still there. I believe that she was on the same team even last year, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Dr. Stakic hired anybody of non-Serb ethnicity in 1993 or 1994?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: I think so. Nevresa Smitran is the lady's name. She is a laboratory technician of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Mrs. Smitran's father die in that period?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Dr. Stakic try to help her in any way under those unfortunate circumstances?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, when Nevresa returned from Tuzla, we actually didn't know when it was when her father died. I believe that it was a weekend, and she went away. When she returned from Tuzla, Dr. Stakic applied our regulations and ordered four salaries to be paid out to her in respect of the assistance for the expenses that she had had at the time. The times were difficult, salaries were low, and that's how he could help her.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anybody of non-Serb ethnicity work within the maintenance of the heating system in the health centre? Whose work obligation was that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was part of the work obligation, but he was an elderly man whose name was Sikman, and there was also another younger man, younger Muslim, whose name was Nihad, and his last name I believe was Muslimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is there anything interesting about the position of that man in the health centre?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: He was treated like anybody else was. But let me tell you one something: Muslimovic's work assignment was as a military person. Instead of being engaged within the military, the Ministry of Defence assigned him to help with the maintenance of the heating system because the health centre was an institution of a special importance in providing health care. And we were not obliged to pay any such people. However, according to Dr. Stakic's order, who told me personally to issue an order to the accountant who was in charge of paying the meals to all of our employees, that this person Muslimovic would also be on that list of those who would be paid for the meals. I don't know how long it lasted, but for as long as this person was there, he had an employment contract and he received the same remunerations as I did. At the time, I thought it was perfectly normal and okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: With all due respect, please understand, Ms. Dakic, and also Defence counsel, that we have to concentrate on the period of time of the indictment before us. Nobody, nobody in this courtroom alleges that Dr. Stakic ever discriminated a person on the basis of gender or ethnicity out of the period of time alleged in the fourth amended indictment. And this is the period of time in 1992. These points or remarks, they are no doubt extremely important for you, Ms. Dakic, but it has nothing to do with the case. So may I ask, please, Defence counsel, to concentrate on the disputed points and the relevant parts of your examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to some more general areas relative to the period prior to April 1992 and after April 1992. Can you tell us which ethnic groups were in favour of the secession from Yugoslavia, which were in favour of remaining in Yugoslavia, and how did these peoples or ethnicities rally around this issue?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: The first ethnic group or people that opted for secession were Slovenes. After them, the same situation repeated in Croatia, which means that the Croatian people also opted for secession from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Within Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Within Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were the Muslim, the Serb, and the Croats living together. And the Croats, inspired by what had happened in Croatia, opted for the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the remainder of the former Yugoslavia. The Muslims never attempted to hide their desire not to live in Yugoslavia, whereas the Serbs wanted to remain living together with the remaining republics, which were Macedonia, Montenegro, and Serbia. And it was the desire of the Serbian people for the fourth republic in that rump Yugoslavia to be Bosnia-Herzegovina because we were a republic that was rather mixed; it was impossible to draw a line between the Serbs and the Muslims, the Muslims and the Croats, the Croats and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there a coalition of two peoples against a third people, and were rallies organised at the time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. You could see it daily on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period prior to April 1992.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, prior to April 1992, the ethnically based parties were established, the first one being the SDA. And after it, I don't know whether the next one was the Serbian Democratic Party, or the HDZ, I can't tell you for a fact. But the establishment of these parties made it clear that the peoples would -- took sides on ethnic background. And it was sort of awkward for a Serb to be a member of the SDA or for a Croat to be a member of the Serbian Democratic Party. At that time, this didn't seem so bad to us; however, the division was already in place. But you could, for example, see at those rallies a Croat flag or a Muslim flag or it would be an SDA flag or an HDZ flag. Or it would be a state flag. However, when I say "state flags," to my mind, these were party flags because Bosnia and Herzegovina still existed and it had its own flag. However, at those rallies, you could never see a Serbian flag or an SDS flag or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just ask one question: When there were these rallies and campaigning for election, did you see also at that time posters depicting candidates of the parties campaigning for this election?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you also see at that time posters showing Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, Dr. Stakic could not be seen on any posters. The elections in the territory of Prijedor Municipality, as I could see, Dr. Stakic was a member of the radical party, which was closer to me. It was founded by Veljko Guberina. That's Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. how I could remember it better. There were many parties, and I would get confused on their names. In the place where I live, Mr. Guberina's party was established, and the president of that board was Mr. Stakic. And as such, he appeared in the multiparty elections which were held in the territory of Prijedor Municipality. And as a member of that party, he was appointed the vice-president of Prijedor Municipality. And when was it that Dr. Stakic became a member of the Serbian democratic party and whether he ever became a member of that party, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just to conclude this, and I'm awfully sorry, but it's of some relevance, did you ever see, be it in Omarska or be it in Prijedor, posters depicting Dr. Stakic, be it for the one or other party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sorry for interrupting. Please, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you for your help.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The division into two options we're talking about the tying of the flags, so did this division reflect in the political life of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Obviously it did. After the establishment of these parties, the majority of the most respectable people, the leading people in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina, started opting for one of those parties. And in the sessions of the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which were aired on TV so all of us could watch that, one could clearly see that there was no agreement and that there was no unity. Every time the MPs of Serb ethnicity were outvoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that all of the political parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in their platforms, before they were set up opted for the mandatory -- the situation in which Bosnia and Herzegovina would stay in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: I didn't read the platform of any of these parties, but reading the newspapers at the time, I arrived at the conclusion that these platforms were all very similar. And they all fostered democratic views, the desire for unity. None of the platforms actually showed it clearly that the establishment of these parties would result in a clash. At the beginning, it seemed to all of us that this was based on the right of every man -- of every person to their democratic view. We lived in a monoparty system for a long, and it seemed to us that was an opportunity for everybody to express their political opinions. And reading the platforms, no, it never occurred to any of us that these platforms would be at the detriment of somebody else. None of these platforms were really obvious in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know when it was that the SDA and HDZ departed from the proclaimed unity?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know when it happened. But it was clear, it became clear from their behaviour, when that unity stopped existing. To my mind, it happened at the moment when I saw that at the sessions of the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the members of the three peoples could never reach any agreement on anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, this would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 4.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And please, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we continue, Mrs. Dakic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I omitted to ask you, and you failed to mention, do you know whether the buses carrying people who were leaving Prijedor prior to the 30th of April, 1992, do you know which direction, which route, they took?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Well, they left the territory of our municipality. I believe that they went to Germany, Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Via which former republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the 30th of April, you could no longer travel from Omarska to Prijedor via Kozarac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anyone -- was any one of the medical staff killed during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you describe for us what happened.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact date when it happened, but it happened during the war in this part of the country, in the area of Kozarac. Our technician, Blagoje Baltic, went to provide assistance to someone. I don't know who it was. And was killed on that occasion by the members of Muslim units, Muslim people. Whether those were armed soldiers or civilians carrying rifles, I'm not sure. I cannot tell you that. However, I know for sure that Blagoje had gone to help someone in the area of Kozarac. I don't know whether he was supposed to provide assistance to a Serb or a Muslim. But he ended up being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the conflict in Kozarac, which took place on the 24th of May, 1992, did any resident of Kozarac reach Omarska at one point in time? Did anyone from Kozarac come to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a conflict, an armed conflict, between the army and the armed members of the Muslim community on that Saturday or Sunday. I don't know whether it was on Monday or on Tuesday, on the 26th or the 27th of May. But at any rate, from the territory of the village of Kevljani, which was part of the Omarska area but inhabited by Muslims, a number of women and children were brought to Omarska to the community centre there. Most of us knew these people, these women and children, because the children from Kevljani went to school in Omarska from the fifth until the eighth grade of the elementary school. As for the first four grades, they went to the local school in Kevljani.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After a while, did these women and children leave the area of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They didn't stay there for long. It was summertime, and many residents of Omarska knew them. They came to see them and gave them water, juices, because these people were their acquaintances, their friends. After a while, these women and children boarded some buses. What I'm telling you is what I heard from the conversations with the people who were there, and I was told that they were -- that they would be taken to the youth centre in Omarska -- in Prijedor, I'm sorry. And the reason why they couldn't go back to their homes in Kevljani was because there was fighting going on in that area. Whether they eventually indeed ended up in the youth centre in Prijedor or somewhere else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In April and May, did Dr. Stakic travel from Omarska to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: I believe he did; however, I cannot confirm this with certainty because I didn't know everything about Mr. Stakic. When he came to work to Omarska at the health centre in Omarska as a physician, he did live in Omarska, and I think that he was still living in Omarska when these events took place. Whether during the month of May, in view of the fact that it was impossible to travel and that he had his responsibilities as the president of the municipality, whether he moved to Prijedor at one point in time --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you knew that he moved to Prijedor after the outbreak of the conflict and you knew that he lived there from that time on. You are just not sure about the date?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were not that close, you see. I didn't know when exactly he left, he moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Speaking of your relationship with Dr. Stakic while you were colleagues, what kind of relationship was it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a strictly professional relationship. He was a physician there, and I worked at the same medical facility as a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did he tell people what they were supposed to do? Did he issue orders? Did he verbally tell them what to do?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: I never received any written order from Dr. Stakic. All our personal contacts were strictly business. We would be called to a business meeting where he would tell us what needed to be done, in terms of everyday organisation of work. He would tell us calmly in a polite manner what needed to be done, who had to do what, who had to obtain medicines or firewood, whatever, what ambulance had to be sent where, and similar jobs. But he would always speak in a very friendly and polite manner to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was Dr. Stakic ever arrested by some paramilitary forces with whom and on account of what, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were those Serb paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were because those were the only formations -- such formations in the area of Prijedor at that time. But I never discussed the issue with Dr. Stakic. I didn't think it would have been fair and polite for me to ask him about that. All I know was that one morning Dr. Stakic and his driver left. After a while, the driver came back very scared and with his hair cut. He didn't say who it was, but he and Dr. Stakic were taken into custody in the youth centre in Prijedor. Their only comment was something to the effect what they were doing there while the war was going on, why they were not participating in fighting. They were apparently used of having been too meek, to reticent. They had -- were supposed to be more aggressive allegedly. Anyway, the driver first arrived alone with his hair cut, as I said. And then after a while, Dr. Stakic also came back. They didn't cut his hair, but I never asked him what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but for a better understanding, could you please tell us at what point in time this incident happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The incident took place in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [No microphone]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I won't ask you anything about that, therefore. You told us that you had never seen Dr. Stakic on posters. Did you -- except on posters. Did you ever see him on TV or hear him speak on the radio?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1992, in the month of May and later, did you become aware of the existence of a Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Not at the beginning of May; however, later I heard the term "Crisis Staff" while talking to other people. This, however, was not the first time that I had heard of this concept. In the system in which I lived, one often heard of various Crisis Staffs or civil protection Crisis Staffs which were often set up in emergency situations. Since we were in time of war, whenever I heard the word "Crisis Staff," for me, that it meant a particular body had been established in the territory of Prijedor Municipality to take care of things such as power shortages, lines were cut off at that time. And for days on, we didn't have electricity. Sometimes, we didn't even have water because the main water facilities were located in the area of Tukovi. So whenever there was no electricity, we didn't have water either. It was also necessary to organise the work of communal organisations in the area of municipality. So the fact that we had a Crisis Staff, for me, meant that we had someone who took care of everyday life of the population in the territory of the municipality. But I didn't know what tasks specifically they had, nor did I know who the members of this Crisis Staff were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we, therefore, conclude, that you were not familiar with the kind of relationship that the Crisis Staff had with the police, the army, and the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that, but it was not possible for them to be in any kind of relationship with the army because the army was, as it had always been, totally autonomous and independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were an employee of a medical institution?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the war, did active-duty servicemen and members of their families undergo treatments in civilian medical institutions?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were they treated?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: They had special medical institutions. There was a military medical centre in Banja Luka, for instance, where doctors and other medical staff treated active-duty servicemen and members of their families, except in exceptional circumstances, in emergency situations, they could, of course, be given assistance in our medical facility or any other medical facility in Yugoslavia. But at any rate, they had their own special medical facilities where they were treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Srdjo Srdic work with you at the same company where you worked?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since when did you work in the same organisation?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Ever since I became employed there in 1974, and he had already been an employee of the Prijedor health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was your impression of Mr. Srdjo Srdic in May, June, July, or before that period of time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: The two of us never met actually during that period of time. However, I heard news about him from time to time because after all, we would discuss our colleagues at work, so every now and then, someone would tell me about him or about what was going on in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, was he considered to be an important personality in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. I don't know which particular office he held at the time, but I know that he was in charge of certain affairs that were conducted in cooperation with the Red Cross because whenever we didn't have electricity, for instance, we would address ourselves to the Red Cross to provide us with candles or with food when it was necessary, hygiene -- sanitary products and so on and so forth. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when you say "we," who do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to us, employees of the health centre and the hospital in general. Because we at times didn't have adequate equipment or supplies to provide our patients with, so we had to find that somewhere. So we would go to the Red Cross for that purpose. And the persons who were sent from the hospital or the health centre to the Red Cross to get something would often mention Srdjo Srdic. Very often, I must say, that they were not -- these people were not happy with his attitude and the kind of work that he did. Apparently, frequently he refused to give them what they needed, but I personally never went there. I didn't ask anything personally from Srdjo Srdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Nusret Sivac before the war?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Nusret, no, I didn't know him personally. I only knew him by name. I know that I used to see him in town, but I was never introduced to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Sivac wear glasses at the time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To you, as a layperson, did it seem that he was very shortsighted, that these were glasses with a very high dioptry, or were they just ordinary sunglasses?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: No, they were not just ordinary sunglasses. I couldn't tell you exactly what kind of glasses they were, but they were certainly not just ordinary sunglasses, and I couldn't really tell you what his dioptry was. That is beyond me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] This concludes our examination-in-chief, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mrs. Dakic. This concludes my examination-in-chief. I will now hand you over to my learned friends from the Prosecution and to Their Honours, the Honourable Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, if you want, you may start. We will have our next break about 20 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, I'd just like to note the number of the events that Mrs. Dakic testified about today were not included in the Rule 65 ter summary. And on the 21st of November, we had requested in the Status Conference to be provided with the names in relation to the events raised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. I think this shouldn't be discussed in the presence of the witness. It is more or less an internal affair. I'm aware of this. And therefore I will convene as soon as possible another 65 ter (i) meeting. It's absolutely mandatory. We can't proceed this way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mrs. Dakic, you testified today that you were working as a lawyer in the medical centre in Prijedor. In April of 1992, how many people did you supervise?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that you weren't responsible for drawing up the lists of persons to be terminated. Who was responsible for preparing those lists?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: The records were kept, and the person responsible for drawing up those lists was the head of the department or the director of the hospital who would inspect the records, together with his assistant, and he would see who was missing from work and for how many days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you involved in the drawing up of any lists from your department?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: No. I was not the person who had any subordinates. There were no people reporting directly to me. In my work unit, the records on the people who came to work were the director and the head of my work unit. That was part of their duty, and they did that throughout my employment in the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any Serb doctors who were dismissed from the hospital in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: I do. Dr. Vojislav Milosev. In May 1992, he resided in the area of Omarska. He was my neighbour. He said goodbye to us and went to Serbia. He was a native of Novi Sad, and his explanation was that he no longer wished to be there because he didn't feel safe. He, his wife, and his two children left and never returned. He never came back to work to the health centre or to the general hospital of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said you were working in the health centre. Were you working in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: According to its organisational scheme, the health centre consisted of the general hospital, the medical centre of Prijedor, the pharmacy of Prijedor, the medical centre in Bosanski Novi, the medical centre in Sanski Most, and the pharmacy in Sanski Most. So when I say that I worked in the health centre, we were an organisational unit that covered the entire territory and had a certain number of departments or segments, as I've already told you. I worked in the department of general affairs, which were in charge of the administrative work that was needed by all of the departments or institutions that I have just listed for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where was your office located?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: In Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In which building?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: In the building which is close to the general hospital of Prijedor. These were some prefabricated buildings or cabins.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're aware that between 550 and 580 people worked at the hospital, are you not?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And approximately 50 per cent of those people were of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you that for a fact. I have never made an effort to establish that, but it is quite possible. There were a lot of Serbs, a lot of Muslims, there were Croats, but there were people of other ethnicities as well. There were even some foreign citizens, and I can't tell you exactly where they came from. But I knew them by name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And out of all of the Serb doctors that were employed at the hospital, you can recall the name of one doctor who was dismissed because he went to Serbia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: No. Dr. Nikola Jegic also left his employment, was also terminated. If I saw all of the names, then I'm sure I would remember them. As it is, it is very hard for me to remember all of them. As far as I can remember, Dr. Risto Stojanovski was also dismissed, but he complained. He filed a complaint. His case was reviewed, and Mr. Stojanovski and his wife Jasna returned, came back to work, because they had a justification for the time they were absent. Dr. Stojanovski has been retired recently, and his wife, Jasna, I believe still works in the hospital. I believe that she is in the hemodialysis department.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is he of Serb ethnicity or Macedonian? I'll move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: He's a native of Ohrid. He was born in Ohrid, and believe me I never made an effort to establish anybody's ethnicity. We never checked the ethnicity of any of our employees. Believe me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You testified earlier that in late August or early September, you were assigned to work in Omarska. What work unit were you -- I'm sorry, 1992. What work unit were you attached to?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: After that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that you were working as a lawyer at the medical centre. And then in late August or September of 1992, you were assigned to work in Omarska. What work unit were you attached to when you were transferred to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Nothing has changed in my status. The outpatients surgery in Omarska was one of the units of the health centre in Prijedor. And I always worked for the health centre in Prijedor and for the general hospital in Prijedor. And this included the outpatients surgery in Omarska, which was a work unit of the health centre in Prijedor. So nothing changed in my status. I was just assigned to perform some other duties. And during that period of time, those duties were performed in Omarska. Because of the difficult situation at the time, my task was to look after the needs of the Omarska outpatients surgery, because that's where I lived and I couldn't commute. So whenever there was a lack of supplies, medical supplies, or fuel, I was in charge of informing the director of the health centre who would then either ask me to come and fetch the supplies or he would ask the main technician or the director of the outpatient surgery in Omarska, whoever, to come and fetch those supplies that were lacking at the moment and were reported to be lacking at the moment in Omarska. That was actually just an assignment to perform certain tasks at a given time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were working as a lawyer in the Prijedor hospital, is that correct, in the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you testified earlier that you were assigned to work in Omarska in late August or September because they needed "my type of work in the work unit." Did you perform any legal tasks within the Omarska outpatients' clinic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. But that's that. That's what I always did. My legal work at the time in Omarska was to maintain the record of the attendance of nurses. Then in consultation with the director of the outpatient surgery, we had to put together the rota of doctors so that the work could be organised. There were not enough doctors to work around the clock. Still, somebody had to be on call in the case of any emergency. So that was my work.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the Omarska outpatients' clinic for?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Up to May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Before you were assigned to the Omarska outpatients' clinic, what legal work were you doing within the Prijedor medical centre from April 1992 until late August 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: My work consisted of the following: During that period of time, due to the fact that a lot of our Muslim staff had - and Croat staff - had left Prijedor, their apartments were vacant. In order to protect these apartments from looting and from other such things, my chief gave me the task to go and make rounds of these apartments to put together the record the condition in which the apartments were found. And pursuant to the decision of the housing committee that was in charge of the allocation of these apartments, I was in charge of putting together the document on the temporary use of those apartments during the time while the circumstances of that nature were in place. Pursuant to such documents, the majority of our employees were able to use these apartments up to the moment when the ministry for the displaced persons and refugees issued a decree on the return of these apartments that were eventually -- have been returned to the previous owners within the past year or two. In the meantime, these apartments have been purchased by their tenants. During that period of time, that is, in 1992, I was also in charge of drafting the legal acts. One of them was the organisation of staffing table, and I did that together with a colleague of mine. I have already told you that the number of work places is not the same in the wartime as it is in the peacetime. And the proposal of this document was always given by the director, so that the director was in charge of proposing this document, and we were just the executors. And we had to draft the document and then we would give that document to our director to sign. He would then check it and see whether everything is within his -- according to his instructions, and then he would sign the document if that document was in keeping with the then prevailing law.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say "the proposal of this document was always given by the director," what proposal are you referring to? You're talking about the staffing table. Is this dismissing certain staff?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid you haven't understood what I meant. When staffing tables are drafted, no names, specific names are mentioned. It is done in the following way, for instance: The general hospital needs during this period of time five surgeons or two surgeons depending on the situation; two internal medicine specialists; two gynecologists; and so on and so forth. When you do this, you do not necessarily refer to specific people. There is a specific number of staff members that are necessary. For instance, each physician requires two assistants or paramedics or technicians, whatever you call them. And by calculating the number of physicians, you can easily calculate the number of paramedics. And the director decides whether he needs five ambulance drivers, for instance, or three or six other administrative workers. In times of war, the situation might change, and so on and so forth. When this proposal, this draft, is adopted, then a final staffing table with specific names of the relevant incumbents of these posts is done. That's how it was done, and that's how it is still done today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Going back to the function in relation to the apartments, you said that the majority of the employees moved into the houses that had been previously occupied by non-Serbs. What were the ethnicity of these employees that moved into the apartments?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: They were not houses, but apartments, flats, which were built by the health centre, by the medical centre, with the resources that were paid to a special fund by all of us, by all of the employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Let the witness answer the question. We had that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, but it was no answer to the question. Therefore, it's correct that there was an interruption. Otherwise, I would have done this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I wouldn't have interrupted the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Madam, there must have been a mistranslation, because I did say "apartments." What was the ethnicity of the persons that were placed into the apartments that were previously occupied by Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Of Serb ethnicity, of course, as a result of the general displacement of the population. Mostly Serb employees remained, and some of these people did not have adequate accommodation, adequate apartments. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And in 1992, in June or July, a special commission, a special board, housing board, was established which drew up a list of all these vacant apartments and made a bidding for these apartments. And the employees who did not have apartments and who considered themselves to be entitled to accommodation applied for these apartments. The board then made a selection, evaluated all these cases, and eventually allocated these apartments. The relevant decision read, I believe, that the apartments were allocated for a temporary use, and so on and so forth. None of these apartments was given to anyone for permanent use. I have already told you that this was done because these apartments had remained empty, vacant. And if the appropriate service from the medical centre had not made an inventory of these apartments, and if they had not issued decisions for temporary use of these apartments, they would have been squatted by other people, people who would destroy these apartments, behave irresponsibly towards the property. And in this way, it was the employees of the medical centre who were allocated these apartments for temporary use.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to move now to another topic. You testified earlier that Dr. Stakic came to the health centre in Prijedor in 1989 approximately. And that he worked in the Omarska surgery until he was appointed vice-president of the municipality. You said that on the 19th of May, 1993, he returned to the health centre as deputy chief executive officer, and you said that on the 1st of January, 1995, he became the chief executive officer of the health centre until 1997 or 1998, when he was succeeded by a new director.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How come you are sure on the dates that he returned to the health centre as deputy and when he became the chief executive officer?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: The date, you're referring to the 1st of January, 1995, and the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that he returned to the health centre on the 19th of May, 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that he became the chief executive officer of the health centre on the 1st of January, 1995.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAVA DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How come you are sure about these dates?
